title_en: MouMou Bank, Shanghai Branch v. Shanghai MouMou Development Bank Co., Ltd., Jinan Branch, et al. — dispute over liability for damage caused by application for property preservation
ruling_gist_en: Applying for a temporary suspension of payment of an independent guarantee is an act preservation. Its review combines procedural review and substantive review, which is distinctive compared to the general act preservation review stipulated in the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC. In view of the institutional value of 'payable upon demand' of independent guarantees, the commercial function of 'pay first, dispute later', and the particularity of the procedure for applying for temporary suspension of payment, an applicant applying for temporary suspension of payment of an independent guarantee shall fulfill a higher duty of reasonable care than an ordinary person.

full_text_en:
Dispute over Liability for Damage Arising from Application for Property Preservation between XX Bank Shanghai Branch and Shanghai XX Development Bank Co., Ltd. Jinan Branch, et al.

[Ruling Summary]

An application for a temporary suspension of payment under an independent guarantee constitutes act preservation, and the review of such an application requires both procedural and substantive examination, which is distinct from the general review of act preservation under the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. Given the institutional value of "pay on first demand" under an independent guarantee, the commercial function of "pay first, dispute later," and the particularities of the procedure for applying for a temporary suspension of payment, an applicant seeking a temporary suspension of payment under an independent guarantee shall exercise a higher degree of reasonable care and diligence than that required of an ordinary person.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2022) Supreme People's Court Final Civil Case No. 260

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): XX Bank Shanghai Branch. Domicile: Xuhui District, Shanghai.
Representative: Da Mou.
Agent ad litem: He Aiqin, Attorney at Law, Shanghai He Aiqin Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: He Aijuan, Attorney at Law, Shanghai He Aiqin Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Shanghai XX Development Bank Co., Ltd. Jinan Branch. Domicile: Lixia District, Jinan City, Shandong Province.
Person in Charge: Lu Mou.
Agent ad litem: Wu Meng, Attorney at Law, Grandall Law Firm (Jinan).
Agent ad litem: Zhang Fei, Attorney at Law, Grandall Law Firm (Jinan).

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China XX Bank Co., Ltd. Shandong Branch. Domicile: Jinan City, Shandong Province.
Person in Charge: Zhao Mou.
Agent ad litem: Sun Fanglong, Attorney at Law, Zhong Lun Law Firm (Qingdao).
Agent ad litem: Du Nan, Attorney at Law, Zhong Lun Law Firm (Qingdao).

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China XX Group Shandong Electric Power Construction Co., Ltd. Domicile: Jinan City, Shandong Province.
Legal Representative: Zhang Mou.
Agent ad litem: Jiang Rongqing, Attorney at Law, Beijing Dentons Law Offices.
Agent ad litem: Zhang Yinzhan, Attorney at Law, Beijing Dentons Law Offices.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): China XX Property Insurance Co., Ltd. Shandong Branch. Domicile: Gaoxin District, Jinan City, Shandong Province.
Person in Charge: Hu Mou.
Agent ad litem: Li Ying, Attorney at Law, Shandong Wenkang (Jinan) Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Li Peng, Attorney at Law, Shandong Wenkang (Jinan) Law Firm.

The appellant, XX Bank Shanghai Branch (hereinafter referred to as Branch A), appealed to this Court against the civil judgment (2021) Lu Min Chu No. 36 rendered by the Shandong High People's Court in the case concerning the dispute over liability for damage arising from an application for property preservation between it and the respondents, Shanghai XX Development Bank Co., Ltd. Jinan Branch (hereinafter referred to as Branch B), China XX Bank Co., Ltd. Shandong Branch (hereinafter referred to as Branch C), China XX Group Shandong Electric Power Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as XX Electric Power Construction), and China XX Property Insurance Co., Ltd. Shandong Branch (hereinafter referred to as XX Insurance Company). This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on October 11, 2022. The agents ad litem of Branch A, He Aiqin and He Aijuan; the agents ad litem of Branch B, Wu Meng and Zhang Fei; the agents ad litem of Branch C, Sun Fanglong and Du Nan; the agents ad litem of XX Electric Power Construction, Jiang Rongqing and Zhang Yinzhan; and the agents ad litem of XX Insurance Company, Li Ying and Li Peng, all appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

The claims of Branch A at first instance were: 1. Order all defendants to jointly and severally compensate the plaintiff for losses in the amount of US$49,978,009.9 (equivalent to RMB 327,855,745 calculated at the exchange rate prevailing at the time of filing the lawsuit with the Shanghai Financial Court); 2. Order all defendants to jointly bear the litigation costs of this case.

Facts Found by the Court at First Instance:

I. Facts Relating to the Issuance, Drawing, Notification, and Payment of Guarantees and Counter-Guarantees

On August 27, 2008, XX Electric Power Construction entered into a contract with an Indian Company, stipulating that XX Electric Power Construction, as the contractor, would construct a 1050MW coal-fired thermal power plant in Kamalanga Village, Dhenkanal District, Orissa State, India. Pursuant to the contract, XX Electric Power Construction was to provide an advance payment guarantee and a performance guarantee with the Indian Company as the beneficiary.

Upon the application of XX Electric Power Construction, on December 8, 2011, Branch B issued an advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG741011000015 in favor of Branch C, with a total amount of US$36,517,244. After several extensions and reductions, the expiry date of this counter-guarantee was January 7, 2015, and the amount was US$20,611,788.60. On December 9, 2011, pursuant to the advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG741011000015, Branch C issued an advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG372131100010 in favor of Branch A, with a total amount of US$36,517,244. After several extensions and reductions, the expiry date of this counter-guarantee was December 22, 2014, and the amount was US$20,611,788.60. In November 2011, Branch A issued an advance payment counter-guarantee No. 06611FG000115 in favor of State Bank of India, Bangalore Branch (hereinafter referred to as SBI Bangalore Branch), with a total amount of US$36,517,244. This guarantee also underwent several corresponding extensions and reductions. All the above counter-guarantees stipulated the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees. SBI Bangalore Branch issued a corresponding advance payment guarantee No. 0686111FG0006001 in favor of the Indian Company. After several extensions and reductions, the maximum cumulative amount of this guarantee was US$20,611,788.60.

Upon the application of XX Electric Power Construction, on April 28, 2013, Branch B issued three performance counter-guarantees in favor of Branch A, numbered LG741013000001, LG741013000002, and LG741013000003, with amounts of US$24,344,829, US$11,290,763, and US$47,037,248, respectively. On the same day, Branch A issued three performance counter-guarantees in favor of SBI Bangalore Branch, numbered 06613FG000057, 06613FG000058, and 06613FG000059, with amounts of US$24,344,829, US$11,290,763, and US$47,037,248, respectively. All the above counter-guarantees stipulated the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees. SBI Bangalore Branch correspondingly issued three performance guarantees in favor of the Indian Company. Guarantee No. 0686113FG0006959 stated: maximum cumulative amount US$24,344,829; Guarantee No. 0686113FG0006960 stated: maximum cumulative amount US$11,290,763; Guarantee No. 0686113FG0006961 stated: maximum cumulative amount US$47,037,248.

On November 3, 2014, the Indian Company demanded that SBI Bangalore Branch pay US$11,688,378.24 under the advance payment guarantee No. 0686111FG0006001. On the same day, the Indian Company also demanded that SBI Bangalore Branch pay the full amounts under the three performance guarantees (Nos. 06613FG000057, 06613FG000058, and 06613FG000059) in the amounts of US$24,344,829, US$11,290,763, and US$47,037,248, respectively. The payment method requested by the Indian Company in the demand letter was RTGS (Real-Time Gross Settlement), and it provided its account number.

On November 12, 2014, at 12:24:22 India time (14:54:22 Beijing time), SBI Bangalore Branch paid the Indian Company INR 2,905,117,705 via RTGS. At 16:33:35 India time (19:03:35 Beijing time), SBI Bangalore Branch paid the Indian Company INR 2,887,516,400 via NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer).

On November 12, 2014, Branch A paid SBI Bangalore Branch the amounts of US$11,688,378.24, US$24,344,829, US$11,290,763, and US$47,037,248.

On November 12, 2014, Branch A sent a telex to Branch B, notifying Branch B to pay it the amounts of US$11,290,763, US$47,037,248, and US$24,344,829; and sent a telex to Branch C, notifying Branch C to pay it the amount of US$11,688,378.24. The three telexes sent by Branch A to Branch B each stated that they were "REMINDER NO.6" and that a payment demand "IN ACCORDANCE WITH ITS TERMS" had been received on November 3, 2014. The telex sent by Branch A to Branch C stated that a payment demand in accordance with the terms of the guarantee had been received on November 3, 2014, and that "HAVE SENT VARIOUS REMINDERS SINCE THEN".

On April 15, 2020, Branch A received from Branch B payments under the counter-guarantees in the amount of US$82,672,840, and from Branch C payments under the counter-guarantees in the amount of US$11,688,378.24, totaling US$94,361,218.24.

II. Facts Relating to the Filing of the Guarantee Fraud Lawsuit, Property Preservation, and the Judgment

The complaint submitted by Shandong XX Electric Power Company, dated November 6, 2014, alleged that the Indian Company and SBI Bangalore Branch constituted guarantee fraud and requested the court to order the third parties, Branch A, Branch B, and Branch C, to terminate payment of the amounts under the guarantees in question, and to order the defendants, the Indian Company and SBI Bangalore Branch, to bear the litigation costs. The complaint submitted by Shandong XX Electric Power Company, dated November 13, 2014, alleged that the Indian Company and SBI Bangalore Branch constituted guarantee fraud and requested the court to order the defendants, Branch A, Branch B, and Branch C, to terminate payment of the amounts under the guarantees in question, and to order the defendants, the Indian Company and SBI Bangalore Branch, to bear the litigation costs.

On November 12, 2014, in the case concerning the application for a temporary injunction on guarantees by XX Electric Power Construction against the Indian Company and SBI Bangalore Branch, the High Court of Orissa State, India, issued an order requiring the parties to maintain the status quo with respect to 12 bank guarantees, including the guarantees in question in this case.

On November 14, 2014, the Shandong High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as Shandong High Court) issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-1, ordering the freezing of bank deposits of Shandong XX Electric Power Company held at China XX Co., Ltd. Jinan Tianqiao Sub-branch in the amount of US$100,000,000, upon the application of Shandong XX Electric Power Company for property preservation to suspend payment of the guarantees. On the same day, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-2, ordering: Branch B to suspend payment to Branch C of US$11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG741011000015; Branch C to suspend payment to Branch A of US$11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG372131100010; Branch A to suspend payment to SBI Bangalore Branch of US$11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. 06611FG000115; Branch B to suspend payment to Branch A of US$24,344,829 under the performance counter-guarantee No. LG741013000001, US$11,290,763 under the performance counter-guarantee No. LG741013000002, and US$47,037,248 under the performance counter-guarantee No. LG741013000003 (totaling US$82,672,840); and Branch A to suspend payment to SBI Bangalore Branch of US$24,344,829 under the performance counter-guarantee No. 06613FG000057, US$11,290,763 under the performance counter-guarantee No. 06613FG000058, and US$47,037,248 under the performance counter-guarantee No. 06613FG000059 (totaling US$82,672,840). On April 29, 2015, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-4; on April 22, 2016, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-7; on April 17, 2017, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-8; on April 8, 2018, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-9; and on March 21, 2019, the Shandong High Court issued a civil ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-10, granting the application of XX Electric Power Construction for an extension of the freeze.

Branch A submitted to the Shandong High Court applications for reconsideration of the civil rulings, dated November 28, 2014, May 11, 2015, May 9, 2016, May 2, 2017, and April 18, 2018, requesting the Shandong High Court to revoke the civil rulings (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-2, 6-4, 6-7, 6-8, and 6-9, on the grounds that it had made a good faith payment on November 12, 2014.

In response to Branch A's application for reconsideration of the civil rulings, Shandong XX Electric Power Company submitted to the Shandong High Court a "Rejoinder to Application for Reconsideration of Litigation Preservation" dated April 23, 2015.

The attachment to the speaking outline for the pre-filing hearing in the independent guarantee dispute of Shandong XX Electric Power Company (second lawsuit) contained a ruling of an Indian court, with backup content: the Indian court ruled "maintain status quo on guarantees."

On June 27, 2016, XX Insurance Company issued a guarantee letter to the Shandong High Court, providing a guarantee for XX Electric Power Construction's application for property preservation in case (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6. It stated that if XX Electric Power Construction's application was erroneous, XX Insurance Company would compensate the respondent for losses suffered as a result of the preservation.

On April 7, 2020, this Court rendered a civil judgment (2019) Supreme People's Court Final Civil Case No. 513 (hereinafter referred to as Judgment No. 513) in the case concerning the appeal of the Indian Company, SBI Bangalore Branch, and Branch A against the respondent XX Electric Power Construction, Branch B, and Branch C regarding the foreign-related guarantee fraud dispute: revoking the civil judgment (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6 of the Shandong High Court and dismissing all claims of XX Electric Power Construction.

It was additionally found that during the trial of case (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6 before the Shandong High Court, Shandong XX Electric Power Company changed its name to China XX Group Shandong Electric Power Construction Co., Ltd. (XX Electric Power Construction).

The court of first instance considered that there were three issues of dispute in this case: 1. Whether XX Electric Power Construction was at fault in applying for property preservation; 2. Whether the four defendants should be liable for compensation to the plaintiff Branch A; 3. Whether the plaintiff Branch A suffered actual losses.

I. Whether XX Electric Power Construction Was at Fault in Applying for Property Preservation

Article 103, paragraph 1, of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "In any case where it may become difficult to enforce a judgment or cause other damage to a party due to the acts of one party or for other reasons, the people's court may, upon the application of the other party, issue a ruling to preserve the property of the party, order him to perform certain acts, or prohibit him from performing certain acts; where no application is made by the party, the people's court may, when necessary, also issue a ruling to adopt preservation measures." Pursuant to this provision, applying for litigation preservation is a procedural right of a party. The application for a suspension of payment in this case is a form of act preservation. Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If the application is erroneous, the applicant shall compensate the respondent for losses suffered as a result of the preservation." Damage suffered by the respondent due to an erroneous application for preservation falls within the scope of tort liability. Pursuant to Article 1 of the Several Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Temporal Effect of the Application of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China, civil disputes arising from legal facts occurring after the implementation of the Civil Code shall be governed by the provisions of the Civil Code. Civil disputes arising from legal facts occurring before the implementation of the Civil Code shall be governed by the laws and judicial interpretations in force at that time, unless otherwise provided by the laws or judicial interpretations. In this case, the application by XX Electric Power Construction for a suspension of payment under the independent guarantees, the issuance of the civil rulings for suspension of payment by the Shandong High Court, and the time when Branch A claimed its losses arose all occurred before the implementation of the Civil Code of the People's Republic of China. Therefore, whether XX Electric Power Construction's application for suspension of payment constituted a tort should still be governed by the law effective at that time, namely the Tort Liability Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Tort Liability Law). Articles 6 and 7 of the Tort Liability Law provide that tort liability is based on the principle of fault liability, and liability without fault must have a legal basis. However, the types of liability without fault provided for in the Tort Liability Law do not include liability for damages arising from erroneous applications for preservation. Accordingly, in cases concerning damages for erroneous application for preservation, whether the applicant for preservation should compensate for corresponding losses shall be determined in accordance with the constituent elements of a general tort, applying the principle of fault liability as the standard for imputation. In determining fault in an application for litigation property preservation, the mere fact that the claim ultimately was not supported cannot be used as the sole basis for concluding that the applicant was at fault. Rather, the determination shall be based on whether the applicant acted with intent or failed to exercise due diligence, amounting to gross negligence at the time of applying for preservation. Therefore, only when the applicant acted with intent or gross negligence can it be determined that the preservation application was indeed erroneous.

The court of first instance held that, based on the facts ascertained in this case, the existing evidence could not prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault of intent or gross negligence in applying for the preservation measure. Moumou A Branch asserted that Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for preservation was erroneous, primarily based on the following four reasons: 1. Judgment No. 513 dismissed Moumou Electric Power Construction's claims, proving that its application for preservation was erroneous. Pursuant to Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC and Article 15 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Disputes over Independent Guarantees (hereinafter referred to as the "Independent Guarantee Provisions"), it should bear liability for compensation for losses caused by erroneous preservation and payment suspension. 2. When Moumou Electric Power Construction filed the lawsuit in the guarantee fraud case (Shandong High People's Court (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6), it listed Moumou A Branch, which had no contractual relationship or guarantee relationship with it, as a third party, and later changed Moumou A Branch to a defendant, which constituted malice. 3. When Moumou Electric Power Construction applied for the payment suspension ruling in the guarantee fraud case, it did not provide any evidence to prove that Moumou A Branch was involved in fraud. Without evidence, suspending payment of the counter-guarantee was an improper obstruction of the claim, and the purpose of the preservation was to prevent funds from leaving the country. During the continuation of the preservation, Moumou A Branch had repeatedly applied for reconsideration of the preservation ruling. 4. Moumou A Branch's application to lift the seizure by providing a guarantee in the form of a letter of guarantee was not agreed to by Moumou Electric Power Construction, resulting in expanded losses.

In this regard, the court of first instance gave its respective assessments as follows: 1. Although Judgment No. 513 dismissed Moumou Electric Power Construction's claims, it does not necessarily indicate that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault. The existence of subjective fault must be proved by corresponding evidence. The purpose of legal provisions on liability for damages from litigation preservation is to constrain parties to prudently apply for preservation and to prevent abuse of litigation rights, while the purpose of the property preservation system is to ensure the enforcement of future effective judgments, not to be a final confirmation of substantive obligations. Therefore, when an applicant seeks judicial relief to protect its legitimate rights and interests by applying for property preservation, it only needs to exercise the reasonable and prudent duty of care that an ordinary person should exercise. The outcome of the case should only be considered as a reference factor for examining "fault," not the sole factor. The judgment result is determined by many factors, including the litigation conduct of the parties, their understanding of laws and regulations, and the court's findings of fact and application of law. As a party, Moumou Electric Power Construction is limited by its legal knowledge and ability to analyze and judge legal relationships. The court's judgment result was not something Moumou Electric Power Construction could accurately foresee at the time of applying for preservation. The judgment result alone is insufficient to find that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault. 2. Regarding the issue of Moumou Electric Power Construction changing the litigation status of Moumou A Branch, the court of first instance held that Moumou A Branch was the issuing bank of the counter-guarantee involved in the case and had a direct interest in the guarantee fraud. As the applicant of the guarantee, Moumou Electric Power Construction, based on its own understanding of the case facts, had the right to choose the defendant and to raise claims with a reasonable factual basis. These actions were all legitimate exercises of litigation rights. In the guarantee fraud case, whether Moumou A Branch, as the issuing bank of the counter-guarantee, had made payment in good faith was a focus of trial and a pending issue for both the first and second instance courts. Moumou Electric Power Construction listing Moumou A Branch as a defendant did not exceed the reasonable limits of exercising its corresponding right of action. If this were deemed malicious litigation, it would unreasonably restrict the parties' statutory right of action and contradict the purpose of civil litigation rights relief. This case is a dispute over liability for damages caused by applying for preservation. The assessment of "fault" should be strictly limited to the scope of the "preservation application." The litigation status of Moumou A Branch in the case had no necessary causal relationship with the act of applying for payment suspension and its consequences. Moumou A Branch failed to provide evidence proving that Moumou Electric Power Construction acted maliciously in changing the litigation status for litigation purposes. The court of first instance did not support this claim. 3. Regarding the issues of whether Moumou Electric Power Construction provided evidence when applying for the payment suspension ruling in the guarantee fraud case, the purpose of the preservation, and the multiple reconsideration applications by Moumou A Branch regarding the preservation ruling, the court of first instance held that when filing the lawsuit, Moumou Electric Power Construction provided preliminary evidence of guarantee fraud to the court and submitted counter-guarantees to prove the fact that Moumou A Branch, Moumou B Branch, and Moumou C Branch had provided counter-guarantees. Moumou Electric Power Construction's claim to suspend payment of the counter-guarantees due to guarantee fraud was consistent with common sense. Upon review, when Moumou Electric Power Construction applied to the Shandong High People's Court for preservation and payment suspension, Moumou A Branch had not yet made external payment. Only after the preservation ruling was served did Moumou A Branch apply for reconsideration to the Shandong High People's Court, stating that it had already made payment. Moumou Electric Power Construction was unaware of this. The parties thus disputed whether the payment was made in good faith. The Shandong High People's Court organized a reconsideration hearing, during which Moumou Electric Power Construction submitted the Indian court's ruling maintaining the status quo and raised objections to Moumou A Branch's payment vouchers. In its reconsideration defense, it stated reasons for the payment not being in good faith and submitted evidence it believed supported its claims of bad faith during the subsequent trial. In judicial practice, differences often exist between a property preservation applicant's own assessment of its rights and the court's final determination. It is not uncommon for a party's seemingly reasonable claims to be unsupported by the court. If the law required the applicant's judgment of the legal relationship in dispute at the time of applying for preservation to be consistent with the court's final judgment, the requirements for the applicant's litigation ability and predictive capacity would be too high. To protect its own interests, prevent funds from leaving the country, and avoid difficulties in enforcing future judgments or other harm, Moumou Electric Power Construction applied for property preservation and provided security. This constituted a reasonable preservation arrangement to ensure the future enforceability of its claims. This act did not involve subjective fault. 4. Regarding the issue that Moumou A Branch's application to lift the seizure by providing a guarantee in the form of a letter of guarantee was not agreed to by Moumou Electric Power Construction, resulting in expanded losses, the court of first instance held that according to Article 167 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, which provides: "If the person subject to property preservation provides other security property of equivalent value and it is more conducive to enforcement, the people's court may order to change the subject matter of preservation to the security property provided by the person subject to preservation." The prerequisite for the people's court to change the subject matter of preservation is that the other property must be of equivalent value and more conducive to enforcement. Compared with a guarantee by letter of guarantee, payment suspension was more conducive to enforcement. Whether the preservation applicant agreed to the substitution was an exercise of statutory litigation rights and did not violate the law. Therefore, it cannot be used to find that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault. Furthermore, the parties' raising of jurisdictional objections and the international service of process on foreign parties also increased to some extent the workload and trial time of the entire litigation. Therefore, the extension of the preservation period was not caused by Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for preservation.

II. Whether the four defendants should bear liability for compensation to the plaintiff Moumou A Branch

The plaintiff Moumou A Branch claimed that the four defendants jointly committed a tort and that the form of liability was joint and several liability among the four defendants. Moumou Electric Power Construction's erroneous application for payment suspension should bear liability for compensation for losses. Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch, by maliciously colluding and intentionally delaying payment, should bear joint compensation liability with Moumou Electric Power Construction. Moumou Property Insurance Company, as a professional guarantee provider, failed to strictly examine the guarantee for payment suspension, causing the payment suspension application to be maintained and continuously renewed under the company's guarantee. Under the concurrence of tort liability and contractual liability, Moumou A Branch chose to require Moumou Property Insurance Company to bear compensation liability together with the other defendants.

Regarding whether Moumou Electric Power Construction should bear compensation liability. As stated above, the evidence provided by Moumou A Branch could not prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault in applying for the payment suspension of the guarantees. When applying for property preservation, Moumou Electric Power Construction had exercised reasonable care and did not have intent or negligence to harm Moumou A Branch's rights. It did not constitute a tort. No fault means no liability. Moumou Electric Power Construction is not liable to compensate Moumou A Branch for losses.

Regarding whether Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch should bear compensation liability. Moumou A Branch claimed that Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch had engaged in the tort of malicious collusion and intentional delay in payment. However, for the claim of malicious collusion, Moumou A Branch did not submit any evidence, and the court of first instance did not support it. For the claim of delayed payment, although Moumou A Branch submitted the International Chamber of Commerce's Documentary Instruments Dispute Resolution Expertise (DOCDEX) Decisions No. 343 and 344 (hereinafter referred to as DOCDEX Decisions No. 343 and 344), the four defendants did not recognize their authenticity. In terms of content, those decisions were based on the application of one party and lacked objective impartiality. The court of first instance did not accept them. Judgment No. 513 had already found that the counter-guarantees involved in the case all stipulated the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG 458), but URDG 458 does not define "reasonable time." Therefore, from November 3, 2014, when Moumou A Branch issued the demand notices to Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch, until November 14, 2014, when Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch received the payment suspension ruling from the Shandong High People's Court, the time did not exceed a reasonable period. Judgment No. 513 also found that on November 12, 2014, regarding the case of a temporary injunction on guarantees between Moumou Electric Power Construction and an Indian company and Indian Bank Bangalore Branch, the High Court of Orissa, India, issued a ruling requiring the parties to maintain the status quo for 12 bank guarantees, including the guarantees involved in this case. Moumou Electric Power Construction promptly notified Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch of the Indian court's ruling. Thus, Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch did not have the subjective intent to delay payment. Moumou A Branch's claim that Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch delayed payment before the service of the payment suspension ruling lacked sufficient factual and legal basis, and the court of first instance did not support it. After the payment suspension ruling was served, Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch lawfully suspended payment under the counter-guarantees involved in the case, and there was no tortious act. After Judgment No. 513 took effect, Moumou C Branch and Moumou B Branch performed their payment obligations in accordance with the judgment, without fault or imputability.

Regarding whether Moumou Property Insurance Company should bear compensation liability. During the trial, Moumou A Branch expressly chose to assert tort liability against Moumou Property Insurance Company, claiming that as a professional guarantee provider, it failed to strictly examine the guarantee for payment suspension, causing the payment suspension application to be maintained and continuously renewed under the insurance company's guarantee. For this claim, Moumou A Branch neither submitted any evidence to prove the specific tortious act or subjective fault of Moumou Property Insurance Company, nor could it explain the relevance of Moumou Property Insurance Company's issuance of the guarantee letter to the alleged tortious act. It also contradicted the provisions of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Handling of Property Preservation Cases by People's Courts, which allow insurers to provide guarantees for applicants' property preservation by entering into property preservation liability insurance contracts. Moumou A Branch's claim that the guarantee act of Moumou Property Insurance Company constituted a tort lacked factual and legal basis, and the court of first instance did not support it.

In summary, according to Article 90 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, which provides: "The parties shall provide evidence to prove the facts on which their claims are based or the facts on which they refute the other party's claims, unless otherwise provided by law. If a party fails to provide evidence or the evidence is insufficient to prove its factual claims before judgment is rendered, the party bearing the burden of proof shall bear the adverse consequences." Moumou A Branch failed to prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault, failed to prove that Moumou B Branch, Moumou C Branch, and Moumou Property Insurance Company had engaged in tortious acts and corresponding subjective fault, and also failed to prove that the four defendants had a meeting of minds for joint tort. Therefore, Moumou A Branch's claim for joint tort by the four defendants was untenable. Its request that the four defendants bear joint and several liability for compensation for losses lacked factual and legal basis.

III. Whether the plaintiff Moumou A Branch had actual losses

The court of first instance held that the documents on capital increase and the audit reports submitted by Moumou A Branch could not prove the actual losses incurred by Moumou A Branch. Moumou A Branch, based on the return on capital, calculated the huge profits that would have been generated if the funds payable under the counter-guarantees from Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch had been used for investment, and used this as the basis for claiming compensation for losses. The portion of losses claimed by Moumou A Branch constituted expected profit losses. Whether an investment can generate profits is affected by many factors, is not certain, and is unforeseeable. It cannot be simply calculated based solely on the rate of return on capital. There was no evidence to prove whether such losses actually existed and occurred, and they did not constitute compensable losses. There was no legal causal relationship between whether Moumou A Branch increased its registered capital and the act of applying for preservation. On the one hand, it could not be ruled out that Moumou A Branch increased its working capital for business expansion or other needs. On the other hand, Moumou A Branch claimed that the method of increasing its registered capital through the State Bank of India to pay the counter-guarantee amount to Indian Bank Bangalore Branch was a performance of the counter-guarantee obligation. The investment returns claimed in the litigation to be paid to the shareholder (State Bank of India) did not constitute actual losses in this case.

In conclusion, the plaintiff Moumou A Branch's claim for joint and several liability against all defendants lacked factual and legal basis and should not be supported. Pursuant to Article 1, Paragraph 2 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Temporal Effect of the Civil Code of the PRC, Article 6 of the Tort Liability Law of the PRC, Article 103, Paragraph 1 and Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, Article 15 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Disputes over Independent Guarantees, Article 90 and Article 167 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, and Article 7 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Handling of Property Preservation Cases by People's Courts, it was adjudged: All claims of Moumou A Branch were dismissed. The case acceptance fee of RMB 1,681,079 shall be borne by Moumou A Branch.

Moumou A Branch, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this court, requesting: 1. To set aside the first-instance judgment and amend it to support all claims of Moumou A Branch in the first instance; 2. The litigation costs of the first and second instances shall be jointly borne by all appellees. Facts and grounds:

I. The first-instance judgment violated Article 15 of the Independent Guarantee Provisions. 1. This case arose from the dispute over property preservation by Moumou Electric Power Construction applying for suspension of payment of the independent guarantees involved. According to the relevant provisions of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Whether a Party Applying for Erroneous Property Preservation Should Bear Compensation Liability to Third Parties for Losses and the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Laws in Examining Behavior Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes, erroneous property preservation shall give rise to compensation liability. Article 15 of the Independent Guarantee Provisions stipulates that erroneous application for suspension of payment of an independent guarantee shall compensate the party subject to the suspension for losses. Judgment No. 513 dismissed Moumou Electric Power Construction's entire claim for termination of payment under the four counter-guarantees, directly proving that Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for payment suspension was erroneous. As the injured party, Moumou A Branch's request for compensation from the applicant for payment suspension does not require additional supporting documents. 2. Where Article 15 of the Independent Guarantee Provisions already clearly stipulates that compensation must be made if the application for payment suspension is erroneous, the first-instance court's requirement that the injured party Moumou A Branch prove malice on the part of Moumou Electric Power Construction imposed an increased burden of proof on Moumou A Branch. 3. The first-instance court erroneously understood the relationship between the Tort Liability Law and the Independent Guarantee Provisions, pitting them against each other, which was incorrect. This case is a lawsuit arising from a dispute over an independent guarantee and should be governed by the Independent Guarantee Provisions. Article 14 of those Provisions clearly defines the nature of a payment suspension ruling for an independent guarantee as behavior preservation. In addition to meeting the conditions for adopting property preservation measures under the Civil Procedure Law, the people's court must conduct a preliminary substantive examination to determine whether there is a ground for payment suspension, i.e., a high likelihood of guarantee fraud. Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for payment suspension violated the above provisions and should bear compensation liability.

II. The first-instance judgment's finding that Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for preservation to suspend payment of the independent guarantees was reasonable was factually baseless and also violated the legal provisions on preservation in litigation. Moumou Electric Power Construction's application was neither necessary nor lawful. Requiring suspension of external payment after Moumou A Branch had already made payment on November 12, 2014, was impractical. Moreover, Moumou Electric Power Construction's property preservation was not within a reasonable scope and constituted an abuse of rights. In the guarantee fraud case, Moumou Electric Power Construction's claim was precisely to stop payment under the independent guarantees, and its application for property preservation was also to stop payment under the independent guarantees. In name, it was property preservation, but in reality, it was akin to advance enforcement.

III. The first-instance judgment's finding that Moumou Electric Power Construction's payment suspension of the independent guarantees was a judgment error without subjective fault was contrary to objective facts. 1. When filing the guarantee fraud case in early November 2014, Moumou Electric Power Construction did not submit any evidence to the Shandong High People's Court proving that Moumou A Branch had engaged in fraud or acted in bad faith. Knowing full well that Moumou A Branch had already made external payment, it continuously applied for extension of the freeze and concealed from the Shandong High People's Court the Indian court's ruling that the payment on the four guarantees that had already been paid could not be prevented, thereby expanding Moumou A Branch's losses. This constitutes clear fault. 2. In the guarantee fraud case, Moumou Electric Power Construction did not submit the evidence it believed supported its claims until four years after the payment suspension of the counter-guarantees involved, but the relevant evidence was also found by Judgment No. 513 not to support its claims. Therefore, its application for payment suspension was subjectively faulty.

IV. The first-instance judgment's finding that the losses calculated by Moumou A Branch based on the rate of return on capital were not compensable losses, thereby denying that Moumou A Branch had incurred losses, violates the law and objective facts. During the period when the counter-guarantees involved were suspended by Moumou Electric Power Construction, the return to shareholders confirmed by an independent third-party audit firm constituted actual losses that had already occurred. The first-instance judgment's finding that these were not compensable losses has no legal basis. Calculating losses based on the return on capital is merely a method of calculating losses. Such losses certainly include interest losses, losses from the occupation of funds, and losses of operating income caused by the inability of Moumou A Branch to conduct normal business operations. Even if the first-instance court did not consider other losses, Moumou A Branch's interest loss on loans is the most direct. Regarding the interest loss, Moumou A Branch stated in its supplementary agency opinion in the first instance that even if funds were borrowed from the domestic market to complete the advance payment, from November 12, 2014, to April 15, 2020, when payment was received from the counter-guarantee bank, a period of six and a half years, Moumou A Branch's interest loss was enormous (interest loss calculated based on the bank's benchmark loan interest rate for the same period: USD 94,361,217 x 6.1428 (exchange rate) x 6.15% / 360 x 1,979 days = RMB 195,964,913). The first-instance court's failure to protect any of Moumou A Branch's losses was erroneous.

V. The first-instance judgment's refusal to support Moumou A Branch's claim for joint and several compensation liability of all appellees was an error in factual determination.

For providing guarantee for the cessation of payment of the independent letter of guarantee by Moumou Electric Power Construction, a certain property insurance company should bear tort liability. The first-instance judgment held that Moumou Branch A did not submit any evidence to prove the specific tortious conduct and subjective fault of Moumou Property Insurance Company, and could not explain the relevance of Moumou Property Insurance Company's issuance of the guarantee letter to the alleged tortious conduct, which is inconsistent with the objective facts. As a company professionally providing preservation guarantee, Moumou Property Insurance Company should strictly follow the "Provisions on Independent Letters of Guarantee" and relevant preservation guarantee review procedures when examining Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for cessation of payment of the letter of guarantee and related evidence materials, and must fulfill its professional duty of care. Moumou Property Insurance Company provided a guarantee for Moumou Electric Power Construction's erroneous application for cessation of payment, which constituted gross negligence and caused substantial losses to Moumou Branch A, amounting to joint tort.

The first-instance judgment's finding that Moumou Branch A failed to submit any evidence to prove malicious collusion between Moumou Branch C and Moumou Branch B and intentional delay in payment constitutes an error in fact-finding. Moumou Branch A submitted the DOCDEX 343 and 344 rulings in the first instance, and the first-instance judgment refused to admit them on the ground that they were made upon the application of one party, which lacks a basis. The conclusion of those rulings was that the reasonable time after November 3, 2014 should be no later than November 10, 2014, i.e., five working days after November 3, 2014. After Moumou Branch C and Moumou Branch B had issued notices to Moumou Electric Power Construction for payment under the independent counter-guarantee, they knew that their payment obligations had become due but delayed without justifiable reason. Subjectively, they intended to delay, thereby enabling Moumou Electric Power Construction to commit the tortious act, and they were negligent, constituting joint tort and should bear liability.

In summary, Moumou Electric Power Construction's erroneous application for cessation of payment of the independent letter of guarantee caused substantial losses to Moumou Branch A. Moumou Property Insurance Company, Moumou Branch C, and Moumou Branch B are joint tortfeasors and should jointly compensate Moumou Branch A for its losses.

Moumou Electric Power Construction argued in defense: First, Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for preservation does not constitute tort liability for erroneous application for preservation. (A) Tort liability for erroneous application for preservation is fault-based liability, not the no-fault liability under the Tort Liability Law, and requires subjective fault on the part of the preservation applicant. Regarding the determination of fault, because the legal knowledge, ability to prove facts, and ability to analyze and judge legal relationships of the parties vary, and generally do not reach the professional level required for judicial adjudication, whether the litigation claims are fully supported by the court is merely a prerequisite for determining whether the preservation applicant was at fault. Only when the exercise of rights is improper and causes property loss to others should compensation liability for preservation errors be borne based on the principle of fault. The relevant provisions of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning Whether a Party Applying for Property Preservation Should Bear Compensation Liability for Losses Caused to a Third Party" and the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Review of Preservation of Conduct in Intellectual Property Dispute Cases" are irrelevant to this case. Therefore, Moumou Branch A's assertion that the dismissal of all of Moumou Electric Power Construction's claims in Judgment No. 513 can establish malicious litigation and erroneous preservation, without requiring subjective fault of the preservation applicant, lacks legal basis. (B) Moumou Branch A bears the burden of proving that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault in applying for preservation. There is no statutory provision for reversal of the burden of proof in disputes over tort liability for erroneous preservation application. According to Article 90 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China," Moumou Branch A, as the plaintiff, naturally bears the burden of proving that Moumou Electric Power Construction acted with subjective fault in applying for cessation of payment; otherwise, it will bear the adverse litigation consequences. Moumou Branch A's claim that the first-instance court improperly increased its burden of proof is unfounded. (C) The first-instance court correctly applied both the Tort Liability Law and the "Provisions on Independent Letters of Guarantee" simultaneously without treating them as contradictory. The first-instance court's determination under the Tort Liability Law that Moumou Electric Power Construction's preservation application was not erroneous and that it should not compensate for losses complies with the law.

Second, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Electric Power Construction was not at fault in applying for preservation. In a letter of guarantee fraud case, Moumou Electric Power Construction applied to the court at the location of the counter-guarantee issuing bank for an order to suspend payment under the letter of guarantee in accordance with the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG), which was consistent with the regulations at that time and also consistent with the relevant provisions of the subsequently issued "Provisions on Independent Letters of Guarantee." There was no impropriety. Moumou Branch A's assertion that Moumou Electric Power Construction should not have applied for cessation of payment of the letter of guarantee has no legal basis. The order to suspend payment under the letter of guarantee is essentially a pre-litigation preservation; its purpose is to restrict the bank from paying the beneficiary under the letter of guarantee, which is a preservation measure, not a preliminary execution. The Shandong High People's Court's ruling to suspend payment under the letter of guarantee was clear in fact-finding and correct in application of law. Moumou Branch A's characterization of the preservation as "substantially a preliminary execution" to assert Moumou Electric Power Construction's malice is a distortion and misinterpretation of the independent letter of guarantee cessation system and the law.

Third, there was no subjective fault in Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for cessation of payment. First, Moumou Electric Power Construction submitted evidence that Moumou Branch A was not acting in good faith in making payment. During the preservation stage, due to the urgency of the preservation application and the particularity of independent letters of guarantee, the applicant for cessation of payment needs to obtain a cessation order within a few working days after receiving the demand notice. Therefore, it was not improper for Moumou Electric Power Construction to further collect and organize relevant case facts and evidence after obtaining the cessation order and submit them during the substantive trial stage. Second, Moumou Electric Power Construction's submission of supplementary evidence at the hearing did not violate the provisions on the time limit for evidence submission. Moumou Branch A's assertion that Moumou Electric Power Construction's failure to submit evidence of fraudulent payment at the time of filing the lawsuit but only at the hearing proves subjective malice lacks legal basis. Finally, the jurisdiction of Chinese courts over independent letter of guarantee cases has no necessary connection with Indian legal procedures. Moreover, the Indian court's ruling has not been recognized by Chinese courts and has no res judicata effect. Therefore, Moumou Electric Power Construction fully fulfilled its duty of care when applying for cessation of payment in the letter of guarantee fraud case. The first-instance judgment's finding that "Moumou Branch A did not provide evidence to prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction acted with subjective malice in applying for cessation of payment" was clear in fact-finding and correct in application of law.

Fourth, the first-instance judgment's rejection of Moumou Branch A's claim for calculating losses based on capital return rate was sufficiently supported by facts and law. (A) There was no loss due to capital occupation for State Bank of India and Moumou Branch A. The funds under the independent letter of guarantee in question had been refunded by the owner in 2014, so there was no actual capital occupation by State Bank of India. The fund flow between Moumou Branch A and the Bangalore Branch of State Bank of India was essentially a flow between different branches of State Bank of India, and there was no situation of advance payment. According to Article 1 of the "Decision of the State Council on Amending the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on the Administration of Foreign-Funded Banks" [State Council Decree No. 657 (2014)], the working capital allocated by the head office of State Bank of India to Moumou Branch A should be interest-free, and Moumou Branch A suffered no loss. (B) Assuming that the preservation was erroneous and Moumou Branch A suffered actual losses, calculating losses based on capital return rate has no factual or legal basis. First, there is no causal link between the loss claimed by Moumou Branch A due to capital increase and the preservation error. Second, Moumou Branch A's claim for calculating capital occupation losses based on capital return rate has no factual or legal basis. On one hand, it did not provide data supporting the calculation of capital return rate, so it lacks authenticity; on the other hand, using capital return rate as the basis for calculating losses ignores the uniqueness of each capital investment. Even if Moumou Branch A's use of capital to pay the counter-guarantee was an inevitable result of Moumou Electric Power Construction's cessation of payment, that capital might have incurred losses if invested during the period from November 2014 to April 2020. Even if there were possible gains from the occupied capital, such gains are highly uncertain and do not constitute "actual losses" as claimed by Moumou Branch A. Therefore, it is unreasonable to calculate losses from the occupied capital based on the capital return rate of other funds. Even if Moumou Branch A suffered actual losses from the advance payment, the losses should be interest losses during the period of capital occupation. Since the currencies involved in the letter of guarantee and counter-guarantee were US dollars, the interest rate for calculating losses should not exceed the US dollar loan interest rate for the same period. Finally, the period for foreign service of process and the period for hearing jurisdictional objections should not be included in the period of capital occupation. From November 14, 2014, when the Shandong High People's Court began the foreign service of process in the letter of guarantee fraud case, to July 31, 2018, when the Supreme People's Court issued Civil Ruling No. 155 (2018) dismissing the appeal on the jurisdictional objection, this period was consumed by the foreign service process and the jurisdictional objection raised by an Indian company, not caused by Moumou Electric Power Construction. Therefore, it should not be included in the capital occupation period.

In summary, the first-instance judgment was clear in fact-finding and correct in application of law. Moumou Branch A's grounds for appeal are unfounded. It is requested that Moumou Branch A's appeal be dismissed and the original judgment be affirmed.

Moumou Branch B argued in defense: First, the first-instance judgment correctly found that it did not commit any tortious act. Moumou Branch A's claim that Moumou Branch B maliciously colluded and intentionally delayed payment cannot be established. (A) Moumou Branch B never had any communication of intent with Moumou Electric Power Construction aimed at harming others' interests. Moumou Branch A also did not provide any evidence to prove this and should bear the legal consequences of failure to prove. (B) In handling the letter of guarantee business involved, Moumou Branch B complied with legal provisions and industry standards, and did not intentionally delay payment. The DOCDEX 343 and 344 rulings were made based on Moumou Branch A's unilateral application and its unilateral statements, and cannot prove that Moumou Branch B delayed. Regarding "reasonable time," URDG 458 does not provide a specific definition. The time Moumou Branch B spent studying the Indian court's ruling was within the reasonable time for document examination, consistent with URDG 458, and there was no intentional delay in payment. Second, Moumou Branch A's claims regarding losses are unfounded. Moumou Branch A claims to calculate losses based on the capital return rate of State Bank of India, but there is no direct causal link between Moumou Branch A's failure to receive the funds under the letter of guarantee and the capital return of State Bank of India. In summary, Moumou Branch A's appeal has no factual or legal basis and should be dismissed.

Moumou Branch C argued in defense: Moumou Branch A's appeal cannot be sustained. The first-instance judgment was clear in fact-finding and correct in application of law and should be affirmed. First, the first-instance judgment correctly applied the principle of fault-based liability for damages in cases of erroneous preservation application. Second, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for cessation of payment of the independent letter of guarantee was not erroneous. Third, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Branch C, Moumou Branch B, and Moumou Property Insurance Company did not constitute joint tort with Moumou Electric Power Construction and should not bear joint and several compensation liability. First, the issue in dispute is whether Moumou Electric Power Construction's preservation application was erroneous. Moumou Branch C did not participate in the process of Moumou Electric Power Construction's preservation application and had no joint tortious intent or joint tortious conduct. Second, Moumou Branch C also did not commit any tortious act of delaying payment. The letter of guarantee and counter-guarantee involved both stipulated the application of URDG 458, which requires the guarantor to pay within a "reasonable time" but does not provide a rigid definition of "reasonable time." From November 3, 2014, when Moumou Branch C received the demand notice from Moumou Branch A, to November 14, 2014, when it received the cessation order from the Shandong High People's Court, this period did not exceed "reasonable time," especially considering the special circumstance that on November 12, 2014, the Orissa High Court in India issued an order requiring the parties to maintain the status quo regarding the letter of guarantee. Third, the reason given by Moumou Branch A in its appeal that the DOCDEX 343 and 344 rulings should be admitted is not valid. Those rulings are not "arbitral awards" as claimed in the appeal. According to Articles 1.3 and 1.4 of the "Rules for the Resolution of Documentary Disputes," "the ruling does not have the legal effect of an arbitral award" and "unless the parties agree otherwise, the DOCDEX ruling is not binding on the parties." The rulings were made without the participation of Moumou Branch C, based solely on the unilateral statements provided by the applicant, Moumou Branch A. The rulings did not examine whether the applicant's statements were true or supported by evidence. Therefore, the first-instance judgment correctly found that the DOCDEX 343 and 344 rulings were formed based on Moumou Branch A's unilateral application and lacked objective fairness, and thus refused to admit them.

Moumou Property Insurance Company argued in defense: First, the first-instance judgment correctly applied the law. Based on the facts found, the first-instance judgment determined whether the preservation application was faulty in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Tort Liability Law, which does not violate the "Provisions on Independent Letters of Guarantee." The allocation of the burden of proof by the first-instance court was reasonable. Neither the law nor Article 15 of the "Provisions on Independent Letters of Guarantee" clearly specifies that a judgment not supporting the cessation of payment is itself an error in cessation of payment and that no-fault liability should apply. Moumou Branch A did not prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault, nor did it prove that Moumou Branch B, Moumou Branch C, and Moumou Property Insurance Company committed tortious acts and had corresponding subjective fault. It should bear the legal consequences of failure to prove. Second, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for cessation of payment of the independent letter of guarantee was reasonable. Third, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Branch A did not provide sufficient evidence to prove that Moumou Electric Power Construction had subjective fault. Fourth, the first-instance judgment correctly found that the evidence provided by Moumou Branch A could not prove actual losses. Regarding the loan interest loss claimed by Moumou Branch A, this was a unilateral change in the factual basis after it had claimed capital increase and capital return rate. Such a change falls within the scope of amending claims, facts, and reasons, which under legal procedures must be raised before the conclusion of the court debate. However, Moumou Branch A stated that it raised this issue in the form of an agent's opinion after the trial, which does not comply with statutory procedures. The first-instance judgment's failure to address this is consistent with the law. Moreover, Moumou Branch A claimed on one hand that it fulfilled its counter-guarantee obligation by increasing its registered capital, while on the other hand claiming that fulfilling the counter-guarantee obligation resulted in loan losses. These two claims are contradictory. According to State Council Decree No. 657 (2014), capital increase is interest-free, so its claim for loan losses has no legal basis. Fifth, the first-instance judgment correctly found that Moumou Property Insurance Company should not bear compensation liability. Moumou Branch A's assertion that Moumou Property Insurance Company, by issuing a guarantee letter, jointly committed a tortious act with Moumou Electric Power Construction and the other two banks is clearly absurd. Litigation preservation liability insurance is a normal business of insurance companies. Article 7 of the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Handling of Property Preservation Cases by People's Courts" also explicitly allows insurers to provide guarantee for applicants' property preservation by entering into property preservation liability insurance contracts. Moumou Branch A asserted that Moumou Property Insurance Company was at fault for not adequately reviewing the cessation of payment application, but it did not submit any evidence. Even assuming, arguendo, that the insurance company failed to conduct a proper review and insured a high-risk preservation, it would bear the possible claim risk itself, based on the insurance relationship, which is unrelated to tortious conduct. Furthermore, the preservation application in this case was made in November 2014. Moumou Electric Power Construction provided full cash guarantee, and only after two extensions did Moumou Property Insurance Company accept the insurance from Moumou Electric Power Construction in 2016 and issue a policy guarantee to the court to replace the cash guarantee. Moumou Property Insurance Company did not participate in the earlier preservation guarantee. There is no guarantee legal relationship between Moumou Property Insurance Company and Moumou Branch B and Moumou Branch C. The so-called joint tort of Moumou Branch B and Moumou Branch C alleged by Moumou Branch A is unrelated to Moumou Property Insurance Company. In summary, it is requested that the first-instance judgment be affirmed and all of Moumou Branch A's appeal be dismissed.

During the second instance of this court, neither party submitted new evidence. This court confirms the facts found in the first instance.

This court holds that the focus of the dispute in this case is whether Moumou Electric Power Construction, Moumou Property Insurance Company, Moumou Branch B, and Moumou Branch C should compensate Moumou Branch A for losses caused by Moumou Electric Power Construction's erroneous preservation application.

I. Whether Moumou Electric Power Construction was at fault in applying for preservation and whether it should bear compensation liability

Article 103, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "If it may become impossible or difficult to enforce a judgment due to the conduct of one party or for other reasons, or if such conduct may cause other damage to a party, the people's court may, upon application of the other party, issue a ruling to preserve the property of the party, order the party to perform certain acts, or prohibit the party from performing certain acts; if no party applies, the people's court may, when necessary, also issue a ruling to adopt preservation measures." Article 108 provides: "If an application is erroneous, the applicant shall compensate the person against whom the preservation is applied for the losses suffered as a result of the preservation." According to the above provisions, applying for preservation is a party's procedural right, aimed at ensuring the smooth enforcement of the effective judgment of the people's court in the future. However, if the right is exercised improperly and causes property loss to others, compensation shall be made. The act of causing loss to others due to erroneous preservation application is essentially a tortious act. The elements for establishing tort liability should be examined, including whether the applicant was at fault when applying for property preservation, whether the property preservation caused losses to the person against whom the preservation was applied, and whether there is a causal link between the property preservation and the loss of the person against whom the preservation was applied.

This case arose from Moumou Electric Power Construction's application for preservation of the guarantee payment in the separate case of Moumou Electric Power Construction v. an Indian Company, India Bank Bangalore Branch, Moumou A Branch, Moumou B Branch, and Moumou C Branch concerning foreign-related guarantee fraud dispute [Shandong High People's Court (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6, Supreme People's Court (2019) Zui Gao Fa Min Zhong No. 513]. Shandong High Court ruled to suspend payment under the four counter-guarantees involved in the case. Moumou A Branch, on the ground that Moumou Electric Power Construction had made an erroneous preservation application, sued Moumou Electric Power Construction, Moumou B Branch, Moumou C Branch, and Moumou Property Insurance Company, requesting joint and several liability for compensation.

Pursuant to Article 13 of the Provisions on Independent Guarantees, which states: "If the applicant, issuer, or instructing party of an independent guarantee discovers a situation as described in Article 12 of these Provisions, it may, before instituting legal proceedings or applying for arbitration, apply to the people's court at the issuer's place of domicile or to another people's court with jurisdiction over the independent guarantee fraud dispute for an order to suspend payment under the independent guarantee, or may make such an application during the litigation or arbitration proceedings," and Article 16(1), which states: "After accepting an application for suspension of payment, the people's court shall make a written ruling within forty-eight hours. The ruling shall list the applicant, the respondent, and the third party, and shall include the preliminary facts found and the reasons for granting or denying the suspension application," the nature of a provisional suspension order for an independent guarantee is a behavioral preservation measure. However, compared to the general behavioral preservation measures provided for in the Civil Procedure Law of China, it has its own particularities, possessing both procedural and substantive examination features. In addition to meeting the conditions for adopting preservation measures under the Civil Procedure Law, the people's court must preliminarily examine whether there are substantive grounds for suspension. The people's court's suspension order must include the preliminary facts found and the reasons for granting or denying the suspension application.

Article 14 of the Provisions on Independent Guarantees stipulates: "A people's court's ruling to suspend payment under an independent guarantee must simultaneously satisfy the following conditions: (1) The evidence materials submitted by the applicant for suspension prove with high probability the existence of a situation described in Article 12 of these Provisions; (2) The circumstances are urgent, and failure to adopt suspension measures immediately will cause irreparable damage to the lawful rights and interests of the applicant for suspension; (3) The applicant for suspension provides a guarantee sufficient to cover losses that the respondent may suffer due to the suspension. If the applicant for suspension requests suspension on the ground that the beneficiary has breached the underlying transaction, the people's court shall not support it. If the issuer has paid in good faith under an independent guarantee issued on instructions, the people's court shall not rule to suspend payment under any independent guarantee that secures the issuer's right of recourse." This provision sets extremely strict procedural conditions for suspension rulings. A suspension ruling must simultaneously satisfy three conditions: first, the evidence materials submitted by the applicant for suspension can prove with high probability the existence of a fraudulent situation as provided in Article 12 of the Provisions on Independent Guarantees; second, the applicant for suspension must prove that the circumstances are urgent, and failure to suspend immediately will cause irreparable damage to the applicant's lawful rights and interests; third, the applicant for suspension must provide a guarantee sufficient to cover losses that the respondent may suffer due to the suspension.

According to the above provisions, considering the systemic value of "pay on first demand" for independent guarantees, the commercial function of "pay first, dispute later", and the particularity of the provisional suspension procedure, an applicant applying for provisional suspension of an independent guarantee should exercise a higher duty of reasonable care than an ordinary person. Therefore, in determining whether Moumou Electric Power Construction was at fault in applying for suspension of payment under the independent guarantees involved, a comprehensive assessment should be made, taking into account the purpose of the application for suspension of the independent guarantees, the preliminary evidence submitted, and whether the claim for termination of payment under the independent guarantees was supported by the court's judgment. In this case, Moumou Electric Power Construction applied to Shandong High Court for preservation, requesting a ruling that Moumou A Branch, Moumou B Branch, and Moumou C Branch suspend payment under the guarantee amounts involved. On November 14, 2014, Shandong High Court issued Civil Ruling (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6-2, ruling: Moumou B Branch shall suspend payment to Moumou C Branch of USD 11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG741011000015; Moumou C Branch shall suspend payment to Moumou A Branch of USD 11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. LG372131100010; Moumou A Branch shall suspend payment to India Bank Bangalore Branch of USD 11,688,378.24 under the advance payment counter-guarantee No. 06611FG000115; Moumou B Branch shall suspend payment to Moumou A Branch of USD 24,344,829 under the performance counter-guarantee No. LG741013000001, USD 11,290,763 under No. LG741013000002, and USD 47,037,248 under No. LG741013000003 (total USD 82,672,840); Moumou A Branch shall suspend payment to India Bank Bangalore Branch of USD 24,344,829 under the performance counter-guarantee No. 06613FG000057, USD 11,290,763 under No. 06613FG000058, and USD 47,037,248 under No. 06613FG000059 (total USD 82,672,840). Subsequently, Shandong High Court repeatedly granted Moumou Electric Power Construction's applications for extension of the preservation order.

First, based on the facts found in this case, all counter-guarantees involved provided for application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG). Moumou Electric Power Construction, as the applicant for the independent guarantees, should have known the rules applicable to independent guarantees, the systemic value of "pay on first demand", the commercial function of "pay first, dispute later", other unique legal issues concerning independent guarantees, and the legal consequences of erroneous suspension applications. Nevertheless, it still applied for guarantee payment suspension and repeatedly applied for extensions, and thus should bear the corresponding legal consequences. Its defense that the parties' level of legal knowledge led to unclear understanding of the independence of independent guarantees and exceptions, the criteria for identifying fraud, and other issues, claiming no subjective fault, lacks factual and legal basis.

Second, from the preliminary evidence submitted by Moumou Electric Power Construction to Shandong High Court when applying for suspension, it mainly included: the underlying contract, the issuance of the guarantees involved, Moumou Electric Power Construction's performance, the Indian company's breach, and the claim notices from Moumou A Branch to Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch. It did not submit evidence that Moumou A Branch was suspected of guarantee fraud. It only stated in the response to the review at Shandong High Court the reasons why Moumou A Branch's payment was not in good faith, and only submitted evidence that it believed could support its claims during the subsequent trial of the guarantee fraud case.

Furthermore, regarding Moumou Electric Power Construction's claim for termination of payment under the involved guarantees, the effective judgment of this Court in Case No. 513 held: "When Moumou A Branch received a conforming demand from India Bank Bangalore Branch, it was obliged to make payment, and it also had the right to claim against Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch. Moumou Electric Power Construction failed to submit sufficient evidence to prove that Moumou A Branch's payment to India Bank Bangalore Branch violated the terms of the counter-guarantees or the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG 458) and constituted a payment not in good faith. The first-instance judgment's finding that Moumou A Branch's telecommunication sent to Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch on November 12, 2014, contained false statements was a factual error. Moreover, whether Moumou A Branch had already paid the Indian company through India Bank Bangalore Branch at the time of sending that telecommunication is irrelevant to determining whether Moumou A Branch paid in good faith. The first-instance judgment's determination that Moumou A Branch's payment was not in good faith lacked factual and legal basis." Subsequently, this Court ruled to set aside the Shandong High Court's (2014) Lu Min Si Chu Zi No. 6 civil judgment and rejected all of Moumou Electric Power Construction's claims.

Based on the above facts, this Court holds that Moumou Electric Power Construction had obvious subjective fault when applying for suspension of payment under the involved guarantees, and it objectively caused Moumou A Branch losses from years of capital occupation. Therefore, Moumou A Branch is entitled, under Article 15 of the Provisions on Independent Guarantees, which states: "If losses are caused by an erroneous suspension application, and the party requests the applicant for suspension to compensate, the people's court shall support such request," to claim compensation for losses. Moumou Electric Power Construction shall compensate Moumou A Branch for capital occupation losses from the date of Shandong High Court's suspension ruling until the date Moumou B Branch and Moumou C Branch actually made payment.

Regarding the calculation of capital occupation losses, Moumou A Branch claimed that losses should be calculated based on the rate of return on capital, including interest losses, losses from capital being tied up, and losses of operating revenue due to inability to conduct normal business. In the first instance, it additionally explained that if the funds were advanced through domestic loans, the interest loss would be calculated by converting the principal of USD 94,361,217 into RMB and applying the domestic bank loan interest rate for the corresponding period. Moumou Electric Power Construction argued on appeal that even if Moumou A Branch suffered actual losses from fund advancement, they should be interest losses for the period of capital occupation.
